newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's provinces slow on gaming industry draw.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's provinces slow on gaming industry draw.

text.p: Post-apartheid South Africa is loosening puritanical restrictions on gambling, whetting the appetite of companies seeking a slice of a new multi-billion-rand industry.
But it may be close to year-end before many gaming houses open their doors for business with most provinces, which have control over gambling, in no rush to issue licences.

Although the eastern province of Mpumalanga expects its operations to open in July, the other eight provinces are seen remaining outside the expected four billion rand ($860 million) a year industry as they bump against their own bureaucracy.
In the meantime, the future of Sun International (Sisa), the leisure group which had a monopoly to run gaming resorts in self-governing black homelands, hangs in the balance.

Until recent legislation, apartheid era laws forbade gaming houses in South Africa, but cards and dice could be had in the nominally independent homelands that Pretoria failed to get the rest of the world to take seriously.
The National Gambling Act passed last year makes provision for 40 gaming licences -- based on a formula of one casino for each million of the population -- split between the country's nine provinces.
Provinces are required to set up boards to draw up criteria for awarding licences, invite bids, choose successful applicants and handle all the paperwork necessary to set up operations.
In return, provinces can claim a gaming levy on some of the casino revenue to be imposed over and above VAT of 14 percent.
The potential riches of gambling has drawn a number of big-name consortia, which include major local banks, hotel groups and foreign firms from the United States to Malaysia.

Mpumalanga last week pipped other provinces in announcing the names of two preferred bidders for three gaming licences. Head of the province's gaming board, Andre Wilsenach, said final licences would be awarded in March and casinos would open in July.
Asked why the region was first off the mark, he told Reuters: "At the political level we had a commitment and an understanding on the contribution that the gaming industry can make to tourism."
Casino consortia tip the population-rich Gauteng province and beach resort haven of KwaZulu Natal as the next regions to award licences.
But Eduard Jacot-Guillarmod, chief executive of the Gauteng gaming board, said bids could not yet be invited as regulations to enable this needed to be passed first by the provincial government.

"I am hoping that by the end of February we will be able to invite applications," he told Reuters, adding that it would take at least six months to complete the bid evaluation process. Successful applicants for up to six licences would be named at the earliest in August or September, he said.

A spokesman for the KwaZulu Natal gambling board said he did not know when bids would be invited or the five licences handed out. He said the board, which was set up earlier this month, had six months in which to draw up bidding criteria.

The Eastern Cape and North West provinces, where the majority of Sisa's operations are located following the incorporation of the homelands in 1994, are even further behind, neither having even set up a gambling board.

Leon Bevan, a spokesman for the North West, said the province's finance executive, Martin Kuskus had publicly given three separate dates for the appointment of a board. "All three dates have passed and we still don't have a board," he said, saying the problem had originally been a shortage of applicants.

Peter Bacon, Sisa's managing director, warned last week that North West-based Sun City, the jewel in Sisa's gaming crown, could be forced to close if its revenue base is eroded by competition from neighbouring provinces.
Sisa shares have been falling steadily amid uncertainty on its future, losing over half their value since the start of last year to trade at 300 cents on Tuesday.
Recently share weakness has been compounded by reports of an expected 40 million rand loss at Sun City in the year to end June 1997 and Sisa's failure to win a licence in Mpumalanga.
